assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened a door to a whole class of tunable correlated and superconducting phases that could not be reached before. The twist angle works as an experimental control knob, and the field is now broad and original. The discovery rests on a clean experimental observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity, which is what I look for.
assessment.attribution: The theory of flat bands at the magic angle (Bistritzer and MacDonald) preceded the experiment, and the decisive experimental demonstration of correlated insulators and superconductivity came from Jarillo-Herrero's group. Eva Y. Andrei's earlier moire STM and flat-band work is also important, but a three-person prize seems the fairest configuration from the supplied names. The first-author experimentalists of the 2018 papers are not among the credited names, which I note as an unresolved fairness question.
assessment.maturity: Many independent groups reproduced the correlated states and superconductivity, and follow-on work (STM spectroscopy, other moire systems) confirms the picture. The microscopic pairing mechanism is still debated, but the discovery itself is secure and the field has grown for years, so recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is not settled.
Credit split between the early theory, the 2018 experiments and the earlier STM work by Andrei is open.
The key experimental co-workers are not among the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators are a new state of matter with protected edge and surface states, and the field has changed how condensed-matter physics classifies materials. The idea has been verified by transport and spectroscopy, and it is a natural follow-up to the topological recognition of 2016 and the earlier quantum Hall prizes, with a new measurable consequence.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele predicted the quantum spin Hall effect in graphene. The HgTe prediction (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) is not among the credited names, which is a real problem. Molenkamp's group made the first experimental observation of the 2D quantum spin Hall edge channels in 2007, and Hasan's ARPES work gave the first 3D topological insulators. I propose Kane for theory, Molenkamp for the original 2D experiment and Hasan for 3D materials. Mele is left out only because of the three-person limit, and that is a hard call.
assessment.maturity: Both the 2D and 3D cases have been confirmed independently over more than fifteen years. Maturity is high and the field is well established.
uncertainties: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are not credited, which leaves the HgTe prediction without proper recognition.
Splitting theory credit between Kane and Mele is difficult.
Whether the 2D and 3D parts should be recognised together is unclear.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks are an invention with a clear measurement payoff: stability and accuracy at the 10^-18 level, which opens tests of fundamental physics, relativistic geodesy and a redefinition of the second. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and its experimental realisation were original and decisive, and the instrument is verified by comparison between laboratories.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice idea and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clock. Ye's group pushed the performance to a new regime and made the key demonstrations. Both names are clear and the pair is a compact, defensible configuration. Frequency combs were already recognised in 2005, so the allocation avoids overlap.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent laboratories confirm the performance, and comparisons between clocks are routine. Recognition is timely because the redefinition of the second is under discussion.
uncertainties: Other early contributors to lattice-clock concepts or ion clocks may need to be considered.
Whether the committee sees it as invention or as incremental refinement of earlier precision measurement work.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single defect spins, especially nitrogen-vacancy centres in diamond, created room-temperature quantum sensors that see magnetic fields and temperature at the nanoscale. This is a tool that lets people see what they could not see before, with applications in materials, biology and quantum technology.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup's group made the first optical detection of a single NV centre spin in 1997. Awschalom's group did much of the coherent control and spin-qubit work in solid-state defects, and Lukin's group contributed the nanoscale sensing and quantum-register demonstrations. Walsworth also contributed to sensing. The four credited names exceed the limit, so I choose the original single-spin detection plus control and sensing. The allocation is arguable.
assessment.maturity: Many groups reproduce the techniques and the field is mature in its basic methods, though the more advanced sensing applications are still developing.
uncertainties: Credit is spread over several groups and decades, and who made the decisive step is arguable.
Applications are developing, so the mature core must be separated from emerging sensing work.
Walsworth is left out by the three-name limit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Metal halide perovskite solar cells reached high efficiency within a decade and may benefit humanity through low-cost photovoltaics. The scientific novelty includes defect tolerance and the strong optoelectronic properties of the material, and they matter for solar energy, which I know from the materials side.
assessment.attribution: Miyasaka reported the first perovskite-sensitised solar cell in 2009, Park made the solid-state cell with long-term stability and higher efficiency in 2012, and Snaith's group demonstrated the efficient thin-film device. The original experiment is Miyasaka's, with Park and Snaith as decisive follow-ups. I want to be absolutely sure about who did the original work, and the early efficiency was low, so this question needs care.
assessment.maturity: The efficiency record is reproduced in many laboratories. Long-term stability, lead toxicity and scale-up remain unresolved, so the technology is not yet mature and some of the benefit to humanity is still prospective.
uncertainties: Device stability is not yet proven for commercial lifetimes.
The 2009 original result gave low efficiency, so the weight of the first demonstration versus the later improvement is disputed.
The work may be seen as chemistry or materials science rather than physics.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The discovery of a high-mobility two-dimensional electron gas at the LaAlO3/SrTiO3 interface showed that new electronic states can be engineered at oxide interfaces that do not exist in either bulk constituent. Later work added gate-tunable superconductivity and magnetism. It is a clear experimental first with many follow-ups, and I know this interface from my own electron-microscopy work.
assessment.attribution: Ohtomo and Hwang reported the 2004 observation, and Mannhart's group showed the tunable conductivity and superconductivity at the interface. The three names are a reasonable configuration, although other groups contributed to the discussion of the mechanism.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced widely, but the origin of the conductivity (polar discontinuity versus oxygen vacancies and intermixing) has been disputed for years, as my own group's microscopy results on oxygen vacancies at this interface show. The interpretation is still not fully stable.
uncertainties: The mechanism (polar catastrophe, oxygen vacancies, cation intermixing) is not settled.
Many applications are still prospective.
My own earlier work in this area may affect my objectivity and should be noted.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Frequency-modulation AFM with the qPlus sensor and CO-functionalised tips allows imaging of the internal bond structure of single molecules, a direct and verifiable way to see atomic arrangements. As a microscopist I value an instrument that opens a door to seeing chemical structure, and the impact on surface science and on-surface synthesis is real.
assessment.attribution: Giessibl invented the qPlus sensor and the atomic-resolution frequency-modulation AFM. Gross, Meyer and colleagues at IBM Zurich demonstrated the molecular bond resolution in 2009. The original invention of atomic force microscopy belongs to Binnig, Quate and Gerber, and I am cautious because the prize is not for a better version of an earlier method.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many laboratories and used widely, so the result is mature. The question is whether it is a new discovery or an advanced refinement of a method that is already recognised.
uncertainties: Risk that it is judged an improvement of AFM and STM rather than an original discovery.
The IBM team beyond the three credited names (for example Mohn, Moll) contributed to the key experiment.
Wider impact beyond surface science is still moderate.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance and then the very large effect in crystalline MgO barriers made spin-dependent tunnelling practical and underlie hard-disk read heads and magnetic random-access memory. It is an experimental discovery with a large technological effect, which fits the requirement that the work benefits society.
assessment.attribution: Miyazaki and Moodera independently reported room-temperature TMR in 1995. The large MgO effect in 2004 was achieved by Yuasa's group and independently by Parkin's group, which creates an allocation problem because only three names can be proposed. I choose the two original room-temperature observers plus Yuasa for the MgO step, and Parkin's claim is a real competing one.
assessment.maturity: The effect has been commercially mature for years and is confirmed by many groups, so it is timely. A spintronics prize was awarded in 2007 for GMR, so the committee may see this as a continuation rather than a separate discovery.
uncertainties: Priority between Yuasa and Parkin for MgO is contested.
The 2007 GMR prize may reduce the room for another spintronics prize.
The theory of coherent tunnelling (Butler, Mathon) is not credited.
